transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maria Gomez (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Nimbus CTO), Sofia Ivanova (ML Eng), Daniel Kim (Infra)

Summary (auto): Deep dive into a recent accuracy regression observed when Nimbus moved from mixed FP16->AWQ pipeline into full INT8 AWQ/GPTQ variants on their on-prem cluster. Focus on entropy-driven layer sensitivity, KV cache warmup/staleness with batching, and safe fallback strategies for production SLOs.

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick intro — I'm alex, ae, and maria our se will drive the technical part. can we do quick round robin intros?
[00:18] Ethan Park: ethan here — cto at nimbus, been hands on with the inference stack. we rolled AWQ across a bunch of endpoints and saw a subtle but material drop in hallucination scores on clinical summarization tasks.
[00:32] Sofia Ivanova: hey, sofia ml eng, i'm the one who runs the evals and pipelines, we've got traces, logs, and a couple of failing prompts.
[00:40] Daniel Kim: daniel infra — i manage the onprem cluster and KMS integrations.
[00:46] Maria Gomez: thanks, hi all. quick agenda: reproduce, layer probe, kv warmup, batching & cold start, fallback plan. we'll capture action items.

---

[02:12] Maria Gomez: so to set context, the regression appeared after switching to the AWQ-INT8 profile using our quant toolchain, and also trying GPTQ for a smaller family of requests. both had different failure modes. AWQ had lower latency but occasional semantic drift, whereas GPTQ kept better fidelity but higher tail latency. is that accurate?
[02:35] Sofia Ivanova: yeah that matches. AWQ reduced p95 by about 30% which was great for our SLOs, but our clinical QA team flagged increased hallucinations at a rate we couldn't accept.
[02:48] Alex Chen: and you mentioned hallucinations — can you give a concrete example, like a prompt + bad output?
[02:55] Sofia Ivanova: sure, we have a case where patient history prompts led to fabricated medication names. i'll share a sanitized example later.

[04:05] Maria Gomez: what we've seen in other customers is that layerwise quant noise interacts with attention patterns on long-context medical prompts. entropy at certain transformer layers spikes post-quant and that correlates with token-level divergence. so we usually run a layerwise entropy probe to find sensitive layers.
[04:33] Ethan Park: can you explain 'layerwise entropy probe' again? is that an internal metric?
[04:40] Maria Gomez: yes, it's a lightweight pass over the model that records distributional changes — like KL divergence per layer of the token logits or of the pre-attention activations. we then rank layers by delta from fp16 baseline to quantized run. high delta layers are candidates for mixed precision.
[05:02] Daniel Kim: interjection — on our infra side, if we flip a subset of layers to fp16, does that require model recompilation or a different kernel? network-wise any perf hit?
[05:12] Maria Gomez: good question. for Redwood runtime we support layer-mixing without full recompile in many cases — it depends on Tkernel availability for that op. there can be a small startup cost for switching code paths but steady-state throughput is usually fine. we should probe on your exact model.

[06:40] Alex Chen: let's talk KV cache. you mentioned some of the divergence was worse for long-lived chat sessions?
[06:48] Sofia Ivanova: yes. multi-turn threads got progressively worse, and when we used aggressive batching on busy periods we saw KV cache staleness — basically keys from previous quant variant runs would be reused and produce mismatch.
[07:05] Maria Gomez: KV cache staleness is a tricky one. two axes: cache format compatibility (quant variant A vs B), and temporal staleness where cache items were generated under different precision settings. our runtime has a cache-tagging feature that can pin kv shards to a model signature so we avoid cross-variant reuse, but if you run mixed variants on the same route you can get warmup mismatch.
[07:35] Daniel Kim: we do run a single endpoint that can route to fallback model when latency spikes. we weren't careful about invalidating kv across variants.
[07:44] Alex Chen: that's a good catch. simple fix is to ensure model-signature tagging or isolate the dedicated pools per precision. but that has cost implications.

[09:20] Maria Gomez: about batching and cold starts — AWQ improved throughput, but the cold-start path suffered since FP16 initializations fetch different kernels. when traffic patterns are spiky your p50 looks good but p99 climbs due to kernel JIT and kv warmup.
[09:40] Ethan Park: we saw that during nightly bursts from some data backfills. latency spikes at midnight.
[09:46] Sofia Ivanova: also, our JIT timeouts cause retries which amplify the problem.

[10:58] Maria Gomez: recommended approach: controlled canary with sticky KV, a short-lived warmup queue to prefill kv for heavy routes, plus a fallback to fp16 for requests failing soft quality thresholds.
[11:20] Ethan Park: fallback to fp16 — that means routing and possibly higher cost. what's the cost delta we should expect?
[11:28] Alex Chen: ballpark, fp16 might be 1.6-2x per-token cost vs optimal INT8, depending on batch size and GPU. but it's predictable and preserves fidelity.

[12:45] Sofia Ivanova: on the quant toolchain: we used GPTQ with per-channel scales for select layers and AWQ global quant for others. we suspect the layerwise mismatch is causing attention heads to misroute.
[13:05] Maria Gomez: mixing quant methods can introduce discontinuities. one technique is per-layer fallback masks: keep top-k sensitive layers at fp16 and quantize rest. Another is per-head quant thresholds but that's more invasive.

[14:30] Daniel Kim: about on-prem constraints: we need keys to stay in our HSM and can't export sensitive logs. does Redwood's private deploy support HSM-backed KMS without agent egress?
[14:44] Alex Chen: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations with no key egress; logs can be configured to ship only metadata or encrypted blobs. we'll follow up with the security appendix.

[16:02] Maria Gomez: ok let's walk through a concrete bisect plan. first step: run layerwise entropy probe across baseline fp16, AWQ-INT8, GPTQ-INT8 variants on a small eval set. capture per-layer KL and token divergence. second: run a controlled throughput test with KV tagging enabled vs disabled to observe staleness. third: layer-swap experiments where top 3 delta layers are forced to fp16.
[16:38] Ethan Park: how long does the probe take? we have a tight calendar.
[16:42] Maria Gomez: for a 5k prompt set it's typically 30-90 minutes depending on compute and batching. we can parallelize across GPUs.
[16:52] Sofia Ivanova: ok 5k prompts sounds fine. we'll sanitize them.

[18:10] Alex Chen: planning notes: we'll need an on-prem test node with same driver stack — Daniel, can you stand up a 4 GPU node with the same CUDA/cuDNN versions and provide ephemeral KMS creds?
[18:23] Daniel Kim: yes, we can. I'll aim for a node with A100-ish equivalence, and we'll lock down network egress.

[19:50] Maria Gomez: quick aside on metrics — use token-level BLEU/ROUGE isn't great for hallucinations. we recommend a mixture of direct-check heuristics plus RAG-aware entailment scoring. we'll provide a reference eval harness.
[20:12] Sofia Ivanova: please share that harness. we had trouble measuring hallucination vs acceptable paraphrase.
[20:20] Maria Gomez: will do. it's in the repo: redwood/quant-eval-harness — i'll include a sanitized link.

[22:05] Ethan Park: another systems question: we currently multiplex different models on the same pool to save GPUs. is isolation required to avoid KV crosspollution?
[22:18] Maria Gomez: if you multiplex different quant variants yes you risk cross-variant cache pollution. you can use model-signature tagging or separate node pools. tradeoff is capacity inefficiency vs correctness.

[24:01] Alex Chen: can you say more about signature tagging? is it per-request header?
[24:08] Maria Gomez: we append a short model-hash to cache keys derived from exact model binary + quant profile. it's automatic in our runtime but you can override to force separation.

[25:30] Sofia Ivanova: we have one more oddity — sometime after long sessions the output repeats or freezes. could that be kv wrap-around or staleness?
[25:40] Maria Gomez: repeats often indicate kv misalignment where positional embeddings or attention indices shift due to tokenization differences or cache chunking. quant noise can exacerbate it. we'll instrument token indices in the probe run.

[27:10] Ethan Park: let's talk guardrails for production. if we detect a quality regression mid-run, what's the automated fallback path?
[27:20] Alex Chen: Redwood supports per-route SLO gating: if quality metric drops below threshold you can route to a fallback model, or degrade output (shorter responses), or fail-open to fp16. Typical is fallback to fp16 for critical routes.
[27:42] Daniel Kim: how fast can routing switch? sub-second?
[27:46] Maria Gomez: routing decision is sub-second; but if the fallback model isn't warm the user will feel a p99 spike until warmup. hence warmup queues are recommended.

---

[29:10] Action recap and timelines — Alex to send security docs, Maria to send probe tooling, Nimbus to provision node and samples.

[30:05] Alex Chen: ok we'll circle back — next sync scheduled in two weeks to review probe outputs. any final questions?
[30:14] Ethan Park: one last item — competitor CloudServe pitched a black-box quant service that they claim "zero-regression" — is that realistic?
[30:28] Maria Gomez: careful with "zero-regression" claims. often they restrict workloads, enforce small prompt sizes, or keep fp16 fallbacks. we'll include a comparison note.

[31:10] Sofia Ivanova: thanks everyone, this was productive.
[31:15] Daniel Kim: thanks.
[31:18] Alex Chen: thanks all, closing the meeting.
